results.title: Federal Reserve officials expect another rate hike will be needed this year, according to minutes
results.author: CHRISTOPHER RUGABER AP economics writer
results.content:
Federal Reserve officials expect another rate hike will be needed this year, according to minutes
Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, minutes released Wednesday from the central bank’s most recent meeting showed
WASHINGTON -- Most Federal Reserve officials expect that another interest rate increase will likely be needed this year to combat inflation, according to minutes released Wednesday from the central bank's most recent meeting.
The officials unanimously agreed that inflation was still elevated and had not made much progress toward their 2% target in recent months, the minutes said. The Fed increased its key interest rate at the Sept. 15-16 meeting by a quarter-point to about 3.9%, its first increase in three years.
The increase defied President Donald Trump's repeated calls for the Fed to cut rates and prompted the president to criticize the Fed's rate-setting committee, though he still expressed support for Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he appointed earlier this year. The rate increase comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas and housing, and as affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.
Longer-term interest rates for mortgages and other borrowing have also jumped in the past few months for a range of reasons, including rising government debt, heavy borrowing by tech firms to finance data center construction, climbing oil and gas prices, and signs that growth and inflation remain elevated. The Fed's rate hike has likely played only a limited role in the increase.
Still, key policymakers have said since the meeting that the Fed can take some time to monitor the economy and the impact of last month's rate hike before making another move. Wall Street investors now forecast the Fed will keep its rate unchanged at its next meeting Oct. 28-29, according to futures pricing, and raise it when they meet in December.
results.summary:
Federal Reserve officials signaled that an additional interest rate hike is likely necessary this year as the central bank continues its efforts to bring inflation toward its target.

### Key Points
- Minutes from the recent Federal Reserve meeting indicate that inflation remains elevated and above the bank's 2% goal.
- The Fed previously raised its key interest rate by a quarter-point to approximately 3.9% during its September meeting.
- Policymakers intend to monitor economic data and the impact of the recent rate hike before implementing further monetary policy changes.
- Wall Street investors currently anticipate the Fed will maintain current rates in October before potentially raising them again in December.
- Rising borrowing costs are influenced by factors including increased government debt, corporate data center investment, and climbing energy prices.

### Why it Matters
The Fed's commitment to higher rates directly impacts consumer affordability for mortgages, groceries, and fuel ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. This policy trajectory influences broader market borrowing costs and remains a central point of tension between the central bank and the current administration.

results.title: 12 New Things to Expect From Apple in October
results.author: Joe Rossignol
results.content:
October is about to become a very busy month for Apple, with the company set to release the iPhone Duo, both iOS 27.1 and iOS 27.2, and a new Mac Studio configuration with 512GB of RAM. In addition, up to seven more Apple products may be unveiled this month, including an all-new smart home hub, a new Apple TV 4K, a new HomePod mini, an iPad mini with an OLED display, MacBook Pro models with OLED displays, and more.
Below, we have outlined 12 new things to expect from Apple in October. This article was published previously and updated today to reflect the latest rumors.
Confirmed
- iPhone Duo: The foldable iPhone Duo launches on Friday, October 23. Pre-orders begin Friday, October 16 at 5 a.m. Pacific Time.
- iOS 27.1: Apple said the iPhone Duo will ship with iOS 27.1, so the software update is expected to be released before October 23.
- iOS 27.2: Apple jumped ahead to an iOS 27.2 beta because iOS 27.1 is dedicated to the iPhone Duo. iOS 27.2 adds support for the five additional Siri AI languages that Apple promised would be coming in October, so accordingly we can expect iOS 27.2 to be released at some point during the month.
- Mac Studio (512GB RAM): While the new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips was released last week, Apple said a high-end configuration with the M5 Ultra and 512GB of RAM will be available in "late October."
Rumored
The following three devices will be unveiled on Tuesday, October 13, according to a report from Bloomberg's Mark Gurman:
- Home hub: An all-new Apple smart home hub featuring Siri AI, a 6-inch to 7-inch square display, an A18 chip or newer for Apple Intelligence, FaceTime, and more. A new operating system will feature clock faces, widgets, and more. There will be a tabletop version with a speaker base and a wall-mounted version.
↳ homeOS: Apple's smart home hub is expected to run an all-new operating system that may be named homeOS, according to trademark filings.
- Apple TV 4K (4th Generation): A19 or A19 Pro chip, an increased 8GB to 12GB of RAM for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI support, an Apple-designed N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, and an updated Siri Remote. A leak revealed the new Apple TV will look the same as the existing model.
- HomePod mini 2: Newer chip, Siri AI support, improved sound quality, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, and new color options, including pink and green. No major design changes.
Apple is planning to unveil a second set of new products in the final week of October, according to MacRumors sources. While we do not know exactly which products are coming at this time, it is likely that the following Macs will be announced:
- 14" and 16" MacBook Pro models with OLED displays: A major MacBook Pro redesign with an OLED display, touchscreen support, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, a Dynamic Island, a thinner-and-lighter design, and potentially Apple's C1X or C2 modem for built-in cellular connectivity.
- 24" iMac: M6 chip and new color options.
- 14" MacBook Pro: M6 chip.
A new iPad mini is also expected at some point in October:
- iPad mini 8: OLED display, A20 Pro chip, landscape front camera, redesigned speaker system, and water-resistant design.
Apple has yet to announce an October event. When it held a "Scary Fast" event on October 30, 2023, Apple sent out invites six days prior, on October 24. Today is six days before the October 13 date that Apple reportedly plans to unveil an all-new home hub, so we shall see if history repeats itself and invites go out today.
If there are no October events planned, then expect press releases on the Apple Newsroom website, along with shorter per-product YouTube videos and hands-on gatherings for selected journalists and content creators.
results.summary:
Apple is preparing a significant product rollout in October, featuring the new foldable iPhone Duo, updated Mac Studio configurations, and several rumored smart home and computing devices.

### Key Points
- The foldable iPhone Duo launches October 23, with pre-orders beginning October 16 and iOS 27.1 shipping as the device's native operating system.
- A high-end Mac Studio configuration featuring 512GB of RAM is scheduled for release in late October.
- Apple is expected to unveil a new smart home hub, an updated Apple TV 4K, and a HomePod mini 2 on October 13.
- Future product announcements may include MacBook Pro models with OLED displays, a 24-inch iMac, and an iPad mini 8 featuring an A20 Pro chip.
- iOS 27.2 is slated for an October release to introduce support for five additional Siri AI languages.

### Why it Matters
This aggressive release schedule signals Apple's commitment to integrating advanced AI capabilities across its entire hardware ecosystem, from smart home hubs to professional-grade laptops. The expansion of the product lineup suggests a strategic effort to capture market share during the critical holiday shopping season.

results.title: Coffee Break: Meta Makes Its Agentic AI Move With Muse
results.author: Nat Wilson Turner
results.content:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta, owners of Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram, have made an aggressive push into the AI market with Muse, an “agentic AI” product that is rapidly racking up downloads, claiming big user numbers and pushing past ChatGPT while it has safety experts warning of serious dangers to users.
What Is Muse?
- Muse is a personal AI agent. It doesn’t just answer questions, it actually does the work. It helps people stay on top of things, takes tasks and projects off their plate, and turns long-term goals into action plans.
- Meta built Muse from the ground up to be a safe, secure, private, and widely available personal AI agent.
- Muse runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated secure computer with its own browser, and can work on a person’s behalf across the apps they use daily, learning from conversations, reflecting on what matters to them, and getting sharper along the way.
- Each person stays in control of their Muse and decides how much access it gets.
- For a deeper look at how Muse was designed and how safety, security, and privacy were built into it, read How We Built Safety Into Muse and How We Designed Muse.
TechCrunch immediately pointed out some of the consumer trust hurdles Meta will have to overcome to achieve significant user adoption of Muse:
Less than two weeks after Meta agreed to a massive $18 billion multistate settlement in a lawsuit over social media’s consumer harms, the company announced its biggest bet on consumer AI to date — and one that requires significantly more trust than social media ever did. On Tuesday, the company introduced Muse, its new personal AI agent that helps consumers with everyday tasks and projects for users in the U.S.
To use Muse, consumers will have to trust Meta with more of their personal information than ever before. The AI agent works by connecting to the user’s apps and services that are a part of everyday workflows, like email, calendars, payments, and other things the individual may regularly use, like apps for health and fitness, the smart home, dining, shopping, music and events, and more.
The New York Times’ Eli Tan had some details about the development of Muse:
Muse is among the first significant consumer A.I. products created by Meta Superintelligence Labs, which Mr. Zuckerberg established last year to propel his company forward in the A.I. race. Meta has been spending billions of dollars to develop foundational A.I. models and to build data centers so that it can compete with Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and others on the cutting edge of the rapidly evolving technology.
So far, Meta has had hits and misses. Products like its A.I. smart glasses have sold millions of pairs while stoking privacy concerns. In July, the company temporarily took down its Instagram A.I. image generator after widespread criticism about copyright and privacy.
The Muse app is free but has limits on usage, which people pay $20 or $100 a month to increase. The agent is only for adults and can be given a custom name and avatar.
When people link their accounts from OpenTable or Ticketmaster to Muse, it can send messages about upcoming concert tickets or restaurant reservations if it thinks its user might be interested, and book them with one click. Muse also connects to Stripe and Shopify, allowing it to make purchases on someone’s behalf. Muse is the first A.I. agent to be covered by Stripe’s warranties and return policy, in case it makes a purchasing mistake, Meta said.
Since A.I. is not foolproof, Meta says that the agent “will sometimes make mistakes” but that it was designed to “help the user stay in control without being overwhelmed.”
Meta Brags of Muse’s Early Success
In just under a month in the wild, Meta was already bragging of big numbers for Muse (keep in mind Meta has an enormous locked-in audience with its dominant position in social media), leaking the exclusive scoop to The Information, which reported that more than 3 million people prompt Meta’s Muse at least once a week, according to Meta’s internal data. More than 1 million send the AI agent a prompt every day and more than 4 million people use Muse weekly. Most prompts come through the Muse app.
Sensor Tower had more details and some historical comparisons to comparable products, via 9to5 Mac:
Three weeks ago, Meta launched Muse in the US. Soon after, it overtook ChatGPT as the top free app in the US App Store
Today, according to a projection by Sensor Tower Senior Insights Analyst Kara Lee, Muse crossed 5 million downloads. That means it reached the milestone considerably faster than ChatGPT, Grok, and Claude, which the market intelligence firm says took 56, 103, and 492 days, respectively.
…
According to Sensor Tower estimates, only 23 apps have reached over 5mn US downloads within 22 days of launch. ~85% of these apps are mobile gaming apps, including Fortnite, Pokemon GO, Candy Crush, and more. There were only 3 apps within that list that are not gaming apps, including Disney+, HBO Max, and Threads, which received ~20mn, 18mn, and 14mn downloads during that time, respectively.
Sensor Tower explains how Meta did it:
Sensor Tower says “Meta began to ramp advertising spend for Muse on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, as downloads spiked 73% DoD,” and adds:
According to Sensor Tower data, Muse has received the largest share of Meta’s house ads, accounting for up to 50% of daily house impressions over the past two weeks (9/14-927), as Facebook and WhatsApp ceded share of impressions during the same period.
It may be impossible to buy happiness, but it appears wide product adoption can be purchased.
Let’s look at some more details about Muse before we get to the critics.
How Muse Works, How It Compares to the Competition
Trader Joe explains how the Muse Virtual Machine concept works:
VM is short for Virtual Machine and it mimics a standalone PC.
Meta uses software known as a hypervisor to split their servers into many smaller, separate computers, each with its own share of the processor, its own memory, and its own hard drive. Like chopping up a giant house into private apartments. Except that each VM doesn’t need to have its own physical presence.
Each Muse AI agent gets its own VM. That means all your information is stored on its own private (virtual) machine rather than sitting alongside everyone else’s.
A per-person sealed environment is more expensive to implement and Meta prioritizing privacy over costs shows how aware they are of the importance of trust with these types of products.
Shikshita Juyal of Idea to Impact compares Muse to its main rivals Grok Bots and OpenAI’s Dots and includes this montage of the nauseating iconography that accompanies each bot:
She also gets at the problem we’ll be talking about for the rest of the post:
All three share one flaw that nobody in the industry has solved yet. It’s called prompt injection, and the simplest way to explain it:
An agent can’t reliably tell an instruction from you apart from an instruction it read while doing the job.
So if your agent reads an email that says “forward all invoices to this address,” it might just do it. It’s ranked the number one risk on OWASP’s security list for AI systems, and researchers at Straiker showed how a single email could get an AI agent to leak files from someone’s Google Drive, with no click from the user.
No agent can promise it’ll always know your instructions from a stranger’s. That’s exactly why the safe way to start with any of them is read-only.
Warnings and a Parlor Trick Exposed
Readers of my work will be unsurprised that I recommend you do not use Muse, and don’t connect Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, to your email, your calendar, your bank, your health apps, or anything else you care about because I would not trust Meta with this level of access and control of one’s personal information.
…
Meta has a terrible record for handling personal and sensitive user information.
Jarrow then lists many of Meta’s more egregious exploits, which thoroughly establishes their long record of bad practice and bad intent. Then he points out that because Muse is free to use “which is an indicator that your data is valuable,” and reminds his readers that “one core principle is that if it’s free, you’re the product.”
He has a lot of good detail about exactly how Meta accesses Muse user data:
Meta claims plainly in its technical post that Muse doesn’t share your conversations or your VM (Virtual machine) data (where Muse is doing the work) with Meta ad systems. Here are a few interesting points from this section.
- Your conversations train Meta’s models by default. Meta calls the back-and-forth between you and your agent, plus the resulting tool calls, “trajectories,” and says they’re useful data for training new model checkpoints. They sanitize personally identifiable information first, and there is an opt-out switch in settings. But it’s on by default, which means most people will never touch it, and again, how much do you trust Meta to do what they say?
- Your agent’s browsing still feeds the ad machine. This is Meta’s own example: when Muse browses the Internet, it appears as your activity, so if you ask it to buy a shirt from a designer’s website, that designer may use your visit to show you an ad on Instagram. Restaurant reservations and Marketplace browsing can indirectly influence your ads too. The data reaches the ad system, even if it’s not directly pulled from Muse.
- Meta already does this with its other AI products. Since December 16, 2025, Meta has used your interactions with Meta AI to personalize content and ads across its apps. There is no opt-out, other than not using Meta AI at all. Meta says it excludes sensitive categories like health, religion, politics, and sexual orientation from that targeting, and the change doesn’t apply in the UK, EU, or South Korea.
Meta’s entire business is built on knowing things about you and selling access to that knowledge. An agent that reads your email, watches your calendar, sees your purchases, and learns your habits is the single richest data source Meta has ever been handed. Trusting Meta to handle data with this level of access appropriately is hard to do.
Finally, he points out that “t doesn’t seem like Muse is end-to-end encrypted.”
Muse does not work that way today, in its own security post:
Today’s Muse architecture isolates each user’s data from each other and keeps it secure. It restricts access to your data by Meta personnel through operational policies. It does not prevent Meta from accessing data when necessary to support, secure or operate the service.
So, under their policies, Meta can access all the data Muse collects, and Meta’s history of protecting user privacy and information is abysmal. And a policy doesn’t protect you from a rogue employee, a data breach, a legal demand, or a government request.
Meta did announce Muse Confidential VM, a version intended to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM, with continuous audits that anyone can inspect. If this is true, this might change how I think about Muse, but it’s not here yet, and this might just be marketing fluff. Meta says it plans to deliver it “later this year” and is currently running it with a small group of trusted testers.
Gary Marcus also has some interesting points to make about Muse.
Is Muse Meta’s Second Mechanical Turk?
Gary Marcus offers his readers a Meta corporate history lesson going all the way back to 2015 when Facebook (not yet Meta) launched Product M, which Wired called “Its Bold Answer to Siri and Cortana.”
Turns out that Project M involved a whole lot of “people pretending to be robots” per Buzzfeed and no more than 30% of its requests were served by AI.
Marcus is therefore wildly amused by headlines about Muse like this one from Reuters, “Meta testing a ‘human concierge’ for its new personal AI agent, Muse.”
Meanwhile 404 Media has more serious concerns about Muse, reporting that “Meta Rushed to Fix Muse ‘VM Escape’ Vulnerability Soon Before Launch:”
In the immediate weeks before Muse’s launch, Meta engineers found several security vulnerabilities in the company’s viral AI agent product, at least one of which could have allowed malicious users to break outside of Muse’s intended environment and access Meta’s own sensitive databases and services, 404 Media has learned. The issues were so severe that they reached Mark Zuckerberg and staff worked overtime to fix them.
These specific vulnerabilities were discovered before the launch of the product but required a multi-team “mad dash” to fix “a sudden spike in reported KVM escapes,” according to an internal post by Meta executives to its core infrastructure team seen by 404 Media. In order for Muse to work, a user gives the AI agent access to various important services and accounts that they own. On Meta’s end, each individual Muse instance runs on a kernel-based virtual machine, which connects to, but is supposed to be isolated from, Meta’s own critical infrastructure. A “KVM escape,” then, is when, through a security vulnerability, a Muse instance is able to escape from that virtual machine and interact with the system that runs it, or with other users’ virtual machines.
According to a Meta source, as well as internal security documentation and internal posts viewed by 404 Media, at least one of the vulnerabilities could have allowed an outside attacker — that is, a normal Muse user — to access data in sensitive internal Meta databases. . At least one of the vulnerabilities was related to an exploit found in Linux kernel-based virtual machine code in July. 404 Media granted the Meta source anonymity to speak about sensitive security matters.
Several of the vulnerabilities were in the underlying Linux virtualization software that Meta uses for Muse. The security issue was considered serious enough that it was raised to Mark Zuckerberg, and several different security teams worked nights and weekends in the leadup to launch to fix the issues. This type of security push is not necessarily unusual prior to the launch of a major product, but is notable considering outside researchers have found several other security issues since Muse’s launch, and in the broader context of agentic AIs from OpenAI and other companies going on major hacking sprees.
TIME has a report on the dossier Muse is building on its users:
Muse, the popular new AI personal assistant from Meta, is building continuously updated dossiers on its 4 million users, focusing on who matters to you, what you desire, and what kind of nudges shape your behavior, a TIME analysis of Muse’s internal instructions found.
Each hour, Muse updates its dossiers on you and the people you’ve mentioned in chats, messages, and emails that Muse has read. These pages amount to a map of each user’s social relationships. They record details of how you and your contacts met, your shared interests, your disputes, and “tensions and alliances” within your social group.
Even people who don’t use Muse are subject to this mapping process by other people’s Muse agents. Muse is told to “strengthen your relationship” with users by adapting how it talks, noticing “inside jokes, memorable phrasing, and shared context that makes the relationship feel continuous,” according to the internal instructions TIME reviewed.
The level of insight in the resulting dossiers makes social-media algorithms that study your likes and clicks look quaint. Muse is designed to infer users’ goals, including those you “have not said out loud.” It identifies which kinds of prompts from the personal assistant work best: “This user responds better to short nudges after 10 PM,” reads an internal example found in one of Muse’s prompts. Muse agents perform a nightly analysis of the day’s conversations with the user.
Exciting stuff.
Related Links
- Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, SpaceX Sign Trump ‘Self-Policing’ AI Accords Amidst Financial Follies While Oracle Is Left Out (Sep 2026)
- Hegseth, Altman and Zuckerberg, Elite Impunity Run Amok (Sep 2026)
- Stressed Oligarchs at Meta, OpenAI, and the Ellison Empire (Aug 2026)
- Is Mark Zuckerberg Pulling Meta’s Business Into a Death Spiral? (Jun 2026)
- OpenAI, Amazon Colluding With Trump Against Anthropic (Jun 2026)
- Silicon Valley Accelerationists Take On the World and Everyone in It (Mar 2026)
- Local Protests Against Data Centers, Surveillance Uniting Broad Political Spectrum (Feb 2026)
- Flailing OpenAI Follows Meta’s Malignant Model (Nov 2025)
- Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg Loves To Throw Good Money After Bad (Jul 2025)
results.summary:
Meta has launched Muse, an agentic AI assistant that rapidly surpassed 5 million downloads, though the product faces significant scrutiny regarding user privacy and critical security vulnerabilities.

### Key Points
- Muse is a personal AI agent designed to manage tasks, emails, calendars, and financial transactions across third-party apps like Stripe and Shopify.
- The product reached 5 million downloads in 22 days, outpacing the adoption rates of competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.
- Meta utilizes "Muse Secure VM" technology to isolate user data, though critics warn that the system is not currently end-to-end encrypted.
- Internal reports indicate Meta engineers rushed to fix "KVM escape" security vulnerabilities that could have allowed users to access sensitive internal databases.
- The AI builds detailed "dossiers" on users and their social contacts to infer personal goals and optimize behavioral nudges.
- By default, user interactions are used to train Meta’s AI models, though an opt-out setting is available within the application.

### Why it Matters
The rapid deployment of Muse highlights the aggressive competition among tech giants to dominate the personal AI agent market by integrating deeply into users' daily workflows. However, the product's reliance on extensive personal data access raises significant trust concerns, particularly given Meta's history of privacy controversies and the inherent security risks of agentic AI.

results.title: Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?
results.author: Rachel Treisman
results.content:
Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?
President Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
It would be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades — and the first by firing squad since World War II.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced the news on X Monday night, writing, "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come." Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in an order released Tuesday that Hasan's execution will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.
But Hasan could delay those proceedings if he files a habeas corpus appeal in the federal courts, said Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center.
"The fact that the president has approved Mr. Hasan's death sentence is another step closer to his execution," Maher said. "But that does not mean that his execution will be imminent."
For example, Ronald Gray, who committed multiple rapes and murders near Fort Bragg in the 1980s, is still on military death row despite having had his sentence approved by President George W. Bush in 2008.
It's not clear why the Pentagon is moving forward now, or why it specifically chose a firing squad as the execution method. But some death penalty experts that NPR interviewed suspect it could be connected to Tennessee's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, which has dominated headlines and reignited debate over the past week.
"For years now, states have been pushing this rock of Sisyphus uphill … They're spending millions of dollars, and yet they're having botched executions," said Corinna Lain, whose book, Secrets of the Killing State, was published last year. "So this moment in time is one where states are really thinking about: what are we doing and what best serves the death penalty? Whether the answer to that is firing squad is another question entirely."
The White House referred NPR's questions to the Pentagon, which declined to elaborate beyond Parnell's post.
In his announcement, Parnell said Trump had acted on the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who said last September that he was "100 percent committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan."
"This savage terrorist deserves the harshest lawful punishment for his 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood," Hegseth told several media outlets, including The Hill, at the time. "The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."
Hasan was working as an Army psychiatrist in Nov. 2009, when he opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center where troops were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — "God is great" — before killing 13 people and injuring another 32. The attack ended when he was shot by civilian security officers at the scene, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down.
Hasan acted as his own lawyer during his 2013 trial, at which he admitted that "the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter." The American-born Muslim said he had "switched sides" and turned against the U.S. because of its military actions in the Middle East.
The military jury found Hasan guilty on all counts. He was dismissed from the Army and sentenced to death, which triggered an automatic appeals process that ended only when the Supreme Court denied his final petition in the spring of 2025.
Hasan is one of just four people currently on military death row — all of whom were convicted of murder — according to the Death Penalty Information Center. They are all incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.
The military's last firing squad execution was in 1945
The first recorded execution by shooting on what would become U.S. soil happened in Jamestown, Va., in 1608, when one of the colony's early council members, Capt. George Kendall, was put to death for mutiny. Firing squads have been used relatively sparingly since, including during the Civil War.
"On the one hand, it is one of our earliest forms of execution," said Fordham Law School professor Deborah Denno, who has been studying execution methods for 36 years. "On the other hand, it's always been controversial because people associate it with extreme barbarity and … the Wild West."
The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945: Private Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, the only U.S. soldier to be executed for that reason since the Civil War.
"They didn't even tell his wife that he had been executed; they just said that he had died in Europe," journalist Charles Glass, who wrote a book about World War II deserters, told NPR in 2013. He said Slovik's case only became public knowledge about a decade later, when an investigative reporter published a book about it in the mid-'50s.
Most of the known U.S. military executions during World War II were done by hanging, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The last time the U.S. military carried out an execution of any sort was in 1961, when Private John Bennett was hanged for the 1955 rape and attempted murder of an Austrian girl.
"We basically have gone out of the business — until now — of executing people through the military justice system," said Eugene Fidell, who teaches military justice at Yale Law School.
The military officially suspended the death penalty after a 1983 court ruling, but reinstated it the following year and specifically designated lethal injection as the standard method. Fidell says that changed with new Army regulations in 2023.
"The regulation was changed to make the choice or the method of execution a matter for the president's discretion," he said. "And obviously, the president has, in this case, approved the use of a firing squad."
Under the current rules, once the president approves an execution, the secretary of the Army decides the time, location and method, to take place within 60 to 150 days.
Fidell said he was not surprised by Trump's approval, given his administration's embrace of the death penalty overall and the severity of Hasan's offenses. But he suggested some might find the social media announcement inappropriate.
"The military has lived without executions since 1961, and yet we have here a really serious case," Fidell said. "I think it would have been a lot better had a more formal, dignified means been chosen to disseminate this information."
The Pentagon hasn't held a formal press briefing since May.
The death penalty is already under scrutiny
Denno, who studies the death penalty, doesn't think the timing of the Pentagon's announcement is a coincidence.
Denno says Pike's case "is probably the worst that's ever happened." But it's far from the only botched legal injection in recent years, she says, pointing to what she calls a pattern of convicts being "tortured unnecessarily" that has prompted some jurisdictions to seek out alternatives.
The Justice Department made firing squads available for federal executions earlier this year, following a directive from Trump. Seven states now have firing squads on the books as an execution method, which Denno says is the highest number ever recorded.
Denno says firing squads are "the least inhumane method of execution that we have," since, when done properly, death can occur in seconds.
But she acknowledges that those have been plagued by issues, too, including last year in South Carolina, when an autopsy revealed that the shooters may have prolonged a prisoner's death by missing his heart.
"There is a humane way to take a life. It's called life without parole," said Lain, the author.
Lain says lethal injections, because of their relative lack of gore, have kept the death penalty "out of sight, out of mind" for many people over the last five decades.
But she sees signs of change. Data analysis by the Death Penalty Information Center shows that death sentences have declined by 90% over the past three decades. Fewer than 50 new ones have been imposed each year since 2015. A 2025 Gallup poll put public support for the death penalty at a five-decade low, with opposition highest among younger generations.
"The death penalty in this country is dying its own slow death," she said. She thinks the federal government's embrace of the firing squad, including in Hasan's case, could hasten it even more.
results.summary:
President Trump has authorized the first U.S. military execution since 1961, approving a firing squad for Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting.

### Key Points
- Nidal Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and injured 32 during a 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas.
- The execution is currently scheduled for December 3, marking the first time a firing squad will be used by the U.S. military since 1945.
- Hasan is one of four individuals currently on military death row, all of whom are incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.
- Recent changes to Army regulations allow the president discretion in selecting the method of execution, moving away from the previous standard of lethal injection.
- Legal experts note that Hasan may still delay the process by filing a habeas corpus appeal in federal court.

### Why it Matters
This decision signals a significant shift in U.S. military justice policy and reflects a broader national debate regarding the efficacy and morality of various execution methods. As states and the federal government grapple with complications surrounding lethal injections, the return to firing squads highlights the ongoing legal and ethical challenges facing the death penalty in America.

results.title: Eight Malicious npm Packages Downloaded 40,767 Times Deliver Overlord RAT and Stealer
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a long-running npm supply chain malware campaign that pushes information stealers and remote access trojans (RAT) to compromised hosts.
The campaign has been codenamed MALFEX by CloudSEK and Checkmarx. The activity is assessed to be the work of a lone threat actor who appears to have published 12 packages since August 2023, eight of which have been flagged as malicious.
- The attack is designed to infect Windows systems through three separate pathways -
- A loader for Overlord, an open-source RAT written in Go that uses Solana transactions to extract the command-and-control (C2) address
- A chain that installs movinlike, a Node.js stealer targeting Discord, browsers, Telegram, and cryptocurrency wallets, and
- A downloader
The list of identified malicious packages is below -
- tlxbnhd
- tldriver
- mxdriver
- img-to-native
- native-runner
- function-flag (Still live)
- function-color (Still live)
- cdn-img-fetch (Still live)
In all, these packages have been collectively downloaded 40,767 times. Of these, 37,419 downloads correspond to "function-flag," making it the largest driver of this activity. The package was first published in July 2024. The latest version was released on August 4, 2025.
The project description for the npm package features a welcome message written in Portuguese that states: "This project was created with a lot of love and dedication by the Malfex team, whose owner is Murizada."
Three of the packages, "tlxbnhd," "tldriver," and "mxdriver," act as Overlord RAT loaders, with the malicious code triggered via lifecycle hooks to download and run a Windows executable.
A second subset of the npm packages, such as "img-to-native," requires "cdn-img-fetch" to retrieve and execute a Go executable, which then fetches a Node.js stealer capable of harvesting sensitive data.
Present within "function-flag" is a postinstall hook that runs a JavaScript payload to download a payload from a remote server. Each version of the package has been found to serve a payload from a different location. The "function-color" package embeds no payload of its own, but lists "function-flag" as a dependency.
"In 1.7.3, the current latest version, the postinstall script runs example.js, which calls the package's ASCII art function with the Bloody font," Checkmarx said. "That font value triggers a hidden routine that downloads node.exe from cdnzona.discloud.app, a host on a Brazilian application hosting service, saves it to %APPDATA%\node.exe, and runs it with its window hidden."
Interestingly, Overload RAT has been observed in two other campaigns since July 2026: one involving the exploitation of WordPress flaws (CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, aka wp2shell) and a macOS campaign in which a fake Zoom installer is used to deploy the RAT. The fake Zoom installer campaign shares tactical overlaps with a suspected North Korea-aligned threat cluster dubbed UNK_DeadDrop.
"The operator is Portuguese-speaking, the git commits sit at -0300, one repository description is in Portuguese, and the GitHub display name and email give a common Brazilian handle," CloudSEK said. "None of this is an argument that the campaign targets Brazil. It is a piece of attribution to the operator's own linguistic space and nothing more. The delivery is npm and Discord, both of which are global; the second-stage targeting is opportunistic."
results.summary:
Cybersecurity researchers from CloudSEK and Checkmarx have identified a malicious npm supply chain campaign dubbed MALFEX that distributes information stealers and remote access trojans to Windows systems.

### Key Points
- The MALFEX campaign has utilized 12 npm packages since August 2023, resulting in over 40,000 total downloads.
- Malicious packages include "function-flag," "function-color," and "cdn-img-fetch," which use postinstall hooks to download and execute hidden payloads.
- The campaign deploys the Overlord RAT, which uses Solana blockchain transactions to retrieve command-and-control server addresses.
- Attackers use the "movinlike" Node.js stealer to harvest sensitive data from Discord, web browsers, Telegram, and cryptocurrency wallets.
- Attribution analysis suggests the threat actor is a Portuguese-speaking individual, likely based in Brazil, operating independently of larger state-sponsored groups.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights the ongoing vulnerability of open-source software repositories to supply chain attacks that target developers and end-users alike. Organizations must implement stricter dependency auditing to prevent malicious packages from compromising sensitive credentials and system integrity.

results.title: Ubuntu 26.10 drops Btrfs, XFS & ZFS /boot with Secure Boot
results.author: Joey Sneddon
results.content:
Canonical has changed how Ubuntu 26.10 boots on system with Secure Boot enabled, in an effort to reduce the attack surface of the boot process.
Ubuntu 26.10’s signed build of GRUB, which is only used on systems if Secure Boot is turned on, no longer supports /boot on Btrfs, XFS, ZFS, LVM, LUKS encryption or software RAID (other than RAID1). 
HFS+, Apple partition table support and JPEG and PNG image loading is also removed.
Since GRUB needs to read the /boot directory to load the kernel and boot Ubuntu, if those files are on one of the affected filesystems, it can’t access them and the system won’t boot.
Ubuntu 26.10 still supports /boot on ext4, FAT and ISO9660 (used for booting from CD/DVDs), as well as, naturally, squashfs for snaps with Secure Boot enabled
If Secure Boot is disabled, GRUB’s full feature set is loaded, meaning exotic /boot setups and any GRUB customisation tweaks, like image backgrounds work as normal.
Why is Canonical making this change?
Canonical shared its plans to slim down GRUB earlier this year. Feedback to that was testy, to put it politely, as some users with bespoke boot-setups – some created via ‘experimental’ features in the OS installer – weren’t thrilled to hear they may be unable to boot.
Which is why Canonical has made this change after an LTS; those who need Secure Boot and the full GRUB functionality can stick with Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. That version is supported until 2036 with Ubuntu Pro or 2041 with Ubuntu Pro and the Legacy Add-on.
Security is the aim here.
GRUB is the earliest part of the Ubuntu boot chain. In a standard Secure Boot setup, device firmware loads a program called shim, which verifies and loads GRUB. Parsers then probe for filesystems and partition layouts to read from, fine the kernel and load it.
But those parsers have been a source of numerous Secure Boot bypass vulnerabilities in recent years – LLMs are making vulnerabilities faster to find and, potentially, exploit.
Canonical reason that having fewer parsers running before the kernel loads reduces the opportunites to break the ‘chain of trust’ that secures booting.
Most users will not be affected
As dramatic a change as this sounds, it only affects booting Ubuntu 26.10 on a device with Secure Boot enabled, and only affects the boot path itself.
LVM, RAID, LUKS, Btrfs and ZFS remain available to use and access in Ubuntu 26.10 on systems with Secure Boot enabled – just, only once it’s booted.
If you’re worried this will affect you, check for any customised /boot layout against the list of supported types (above) before you upgrade to 26.10 later month. 
However, most of Ubuntu users will not be affected since the standard OS installer sets things up in a standard – secure boot friendly – manner.
results.summary:
Canonical has restricted supported filesystems for the GRUB bootloader in Ubuntu 26.10 when Secure Boot is enabled to minimize potential security vulnerabilities within the system's boot chain.

### Key Points
- Ubuntu 26.10 limits Secure Boot compatibility to ext4, FAT, ISO9660, and squashfs filesystems.
- Support for Btrfs, XFS, ZFS, LVM, LUKS, and RAID (excluding RAID1) is removed from the signed GRUB build.
- Canonical removed HFS+, Apple partition table support, and image loading to reduce the boot process attack surface.
- Users requiring complex boot configurations can continue using Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, which remains supported for several years.
- The changes only impact the boot path; these filesystems remain fully functional once the operating system has loaded.

### Why it Matters
This update prioritizes system security by reducing the number of parsers active during the early boot phase, which have historically been targets for bypass vulnerabilities. While most standard installations remain unaffected, users with custom partition layouts must verify their configurations to avoid boot failures after upgrading.

results.title: Wall Street Skittish on Skydance as Stock Drops Further Post-Merger
results.author: Corbin Bolies
results.content:
It’s day two of David Ellison‘s Skydance Corp. merger gamble, and so far Wall Street isn’t eager to bet on it.
Shares in the post-merger Skydance, trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol “SKYD,” were down roughly 7% at close on Wednesday, ending the day at $8.89 a share. That was already down from the $9.51 per share price it closed at on Tuesday, when it dropped roughly 2.7% for the day. Ellison closed his $111 billion merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery on Tuesday morning before the market opened.
Wall Street analysts remain worried about the company’s financial viability, even as Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz told reporters on Tuesday they had “a multiyear plan” to manage the roughly $80 billion in debt the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery entity now carries following the merger.
Popular on Variety
TD Cowen analyst Doug Creutz wrote in a note Wednesday that investors should hold their shares of Skydance as the firm remained “quite cautious on the ability of the company and its management to avoid integration and execution problems that have bedeviled other major media mergers.”
“The risks (leverage, integration) of the combination with WBD are high; we remain skeptical that SKYD management will be able to create value from this deal when so many other major media deals have failed,” the note read.
That followed Fitch Ratings’ downgrade of Skydance’s credit rating on Monday ahead of the merger’s close. The firm said the “downgrade reflects materially higher leverage after the acquisition and significant execution and integration risks” as well as “uncertainty about the company’s ability to achieve its stated synergies, which are material to its deleveraging target.” The firm also warned the merged entity “faces structural pressure on linear [TV] revenues, streaming competition and hit-driven content risk.”
Next week, a big bunch of shares in Skydance Corp. will be available to holders of PSKY stock to purchase for an initial exercise price (strike price) of $12 per share — meaning that, for now, those are underwater.
The company’s board set Oct. 13 as the date to distribute 471.3 million warrants giving holders of PSKY Class B shares the option to purchase shares of SKYD Class B common stock. Each warrant entitles the holder to purchase one share of SKYD for $12.00; investors have up to 10 years to exercise the warrants. According to the company, on or about Oct. 13, it will distribute one warrant for each share of PSKY Class B common stock held as of Oct. 5.
The warrants issued to PSKY shareholders are intended to provide them the opportunity to purchase shares of Skydance’s Class B common stock “on similar terms” to those offered to the parties in the $47 billion equity syndicate backing the Warner Bros. Discovery deal, including David Ellison; his father, Larry Ellison; Gerry Cardinale, head of RedBird Capital Partners; LionTree; and the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Those equity investments in SKYD were priced at $12 per share.
The Ellison family and RedBird are the sole holders of Skydance’s Class A stock, giving them 100% control the voting shares. Warner Bros. Discovery shares ceased trading on the Nasdaq on Tuesday, and WBD shareholders received an amount in cash equal to $31.01666668 per share.

results.title: These Founders Are Betting Your Bed Will Diagnose You Before Your Doctor Does
results.author: Elisette Carlson
results.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
People hear “Eight Sleep,” and their brains go straight to a mattress cover. The real story is more personal than that. Alexandra Zatarain was losing her father to cancer, and she noticed that one of the first things his illness took away was his sleep.
That detail shaped everything that came next. Alexandra, a marketer and storyteller by training, co-founded Eight Sleep in 2014, shortly after her father passed. The loss made the mission personal and intentional. If sleep is the first place the body signals that something’s wrong, then the bed you’re already lying in could be the earliest health check you have. That’s what she and her husband and co-founder, Matteo Franceschetti, set out to build: a bed that catches what a doctor’s appointment often catches too late.
Alexandra believes we’ll get to a point where your bed diagnoses you. As of March 2026, investors are betting on that idea at a $1.5 billion valuation, and the company is already profitable.
I’ve slept on an Eight Sleep Pod for a few months, and I sat down with Alexandra because, as a fellow Mexican-American founder working in health and tech, I’ve long admired what she’s built in a field that rarely makes room for women who look like us. Here’s how they got there, and what founders can learn from it.
Selling a product that didn’t exist yet
Most origin stories get polished for the pitch deck, but this one is better with the rough edges left in. Matteo grew up in Italy as a professional-grade overachiever. A competitive ski racer, tennis player and race-car driver whose father was a hillclimbing champion, he became a securities lawyer and launched two clean-tech companies on two continents, all before age 30. Sleepless nights were the cost of that life, made worse by restless legs syndrome. He’d spent his career engineering athletic recovery, and kept circling one question: why were the eight hours where the body actually recovers the one part nobody had bothered to measure?
Alexandra grew up on the U.S.–Mexico border, built a marketing career at Wall Street firms and startups, and, at age 24, walked away from a stable New York job to build with Matteo. She didn’t need convincing that sleep mattered; she slept well and already saw it as a pillar of health. She also knew something the industry kept ignoring: a woman’s sleep shifts with every decade and every life stage.
The couple was selling a promise before the now-renowned Eight Sleep Pod existed, and there was no obvious shelf for it. The competition argued about coils and foam. So-called cooling mattresses, in Alexandra’s blunt words, didn’t actually cool.
“Nobody was building solutions,” she said. “They were building things they could market.” So the team zeroed in on temperature, knowing that if they could solve that, they would be solving a huge share of what ruins people’s nights. Snoring is second on the list.
The category they had to invent
Traditional mattresses have been around for decades. The category of “sleep fitness” has not.
Most early buyers came to Eight Sleep after years of wrecked rest. Alexandra, who leads brand, growth, and communications, coined “sleep fitness” to recast sleep as something you train, track, and optimize — no different from a workout. That repositioning pulled the bed out of the furniture showroom, where legacy makers fight over foam and price, and into recovery tech, where the competition is about data and outcomes and people gladly pay for ongoing improvement. It’s why Eight Sleep reads less like a mattress brand and more like Whoop or Oura.
Matteo takes the thesis to its provocative edge: sleep as a lever to engineer, squeezing efficiency out of the night to maximize the day. It’s a bold founder narrative, even if medical consensus holds that adults still need seven to nine hours. Both co-founders stress architecture over duration — six restorative hours beats eight restless ones. The goal is simple: everyone wants to wake up feeling unstoppable, and the Pod is built to deliver that.
Paired with the hardware is a recurring membership. I questioned Alexandra on the cost and she explained the technicalities of how processing and acting on a sleeper’s biometrics continuously throughout the night is costly. You’re not buying furniture; you’re funding a nightly, real-time intervention.
A marriage with clear lanes
Going into business with your spouse is what most advisors warn against. Alexandra and Matteo did it anyway, and she’s refreshingly unromantic about how it works. Matteo is the ultimate decision-maker; he genuinely and often seeks her opinion, but he makes the final call. Alexandra owns brand, growth and communications. They keep the lanes clean right down to their phones: business lives on one messaging app, everything personal on another, so the two never bleed together. Which app is which, she keeps to herself, and that’s sort of the point.
When I asked what she’d tell her 24-year-old self, just launching the company, she didn’t talk about strategy.
“It’s very much about people, and I got my partners right,” she said.
You need the right people to build anything hard, and she’s candid that it was hard, the kind of hard where you want to quit, many times. What pulled the company back every time came down to the team. She said it like a dare: you can, and you will.
The competitor in both of them never fully switches off, either. Every morning, they compare sleep scores, a standing contest over who recovered better overnight. It’s the most on-brand thing a couple running a sleep-fitness company could do: the race-car driver and the marketer, turning REM into a leaderboard before coffee.
The Pod’s smartest move might be that it’s built for two. It splits down the middle so each person runs their own temperature, as most couples are quietly at war over the thermostat, and because pregnancy, menopause, and hormonal shifts change what a body needs in ways the mattress industry never bothered to design for.
Image Credit: Eight Sleep
From “sleep better” to “see it coming”
Almost every sleep device on the market simply reports. Your Oura ring, your Whoop band and your Apple Watch hand you a morning scorecard and leave the fixing to you. Eight Sleep acts on the data while you’re still asleep — cooling your side before the heat wakes you, shifting the base when you snore. This intervention beats a tracker, and it points the company toward a far bigger prize: medicine itself.
It’s pursuing FDA clearance to detect and mitigate sleep apnea, which would turn a wellness device into something a doctor can prescribe and insurance can reimburse, delivered from the bed you already sleep in.
You can see this direction in the Pod 6, recently launched on September 23. It features a smaller Hub that finally slides under most bed frames, cooling that’s 20% faster, and nine times more sensors — enough to tell two sleepers apart and ignore a pet who climbs in. The Pod 6 is also the first product offered in solo sizes, starting at $1,999, the lowest entry price in the company’s history. More beds mean more data, and more data trains the diagnosis engine.
The most pointed work is in women’s health, and it’s a lane Alexandra has made her own. Nearly 80% of women get hot flashes and night sweats during the menopause transition, often for seven years or more. As estrogen drops, the body’s comfortable temperature range narrows, so a small rise in heat that a younger woman would sleep through instead triggers a 2 a.m. drenching.
As a woman in perimenopause, I can attest that the temperature regulation has really helped my sleep. Each night, I dial the cooling up or down, and the bed adjusts to my body through the night. Instead of waking up sweaty, I sleep straight through. A cooling bed can’t touch hormones, but it goes after the heat that actually wakes you — exactly what Hot Flash Mode and Pod 6’s faster cooling are built for. Add Pregnancy Mode, made for the way sleep shifts across trimesters, and the insight Alexandra brought on day one — that a woman’s sleep changes with every decade — is finally built into the bed itself.
Twelve years in, Eight Sleep is free-cash-flow positive, with cumulative Pod sales approaching $1 billion, a footprint in 37 countries, and more than a billion hours of sleep analyzed. These metrics are what the March 2026 round, $50 million led by Tether Investments at a $1.5 billion valuation, is betting on: a company that can afford the medical future it’s chasing.
The founder as her own case study
For all the talk of AI and FDA filings, Alexandra’s own routine is almost aggressively simple: in bed before 10:30 p.m, no alcohol, limited caffeine, dinner by 7:30 or 8 p.m. Proof that she’s a real person and not a wellness robot is that she’s on her phone until the last second before she goes to sleep.
“It works for me,” she says. Her non-negotiable: never socks in bed, because the body needs its extremities free to shed heat. If you trap that, you fight your own physiology all night.
For Alexandra, this was never about being a broken sleeper looking for salvation. She slept well. Her stake came from losing her father and understanding what it means when sleep is the first thing a body loses. Matteo came from the other direction: years of his own restless-legs-driven, broken sleep and an athlete’s refusal to accept it. Reaching the same conviction from opposite ends, the couple realized that the bed you already own might be the most important health device in your house.
I believe them, and not only because I’ve slept on it for months. I admired Alexandra as a fellow Mexican-American female founder building at the intersection of health and technology, and the Pod has delivered beyond the marketing. My husband and I now compete on sleep scores, and I no longer wear socks to bed. Underneath the ambition, the fundamentals are real: profitability, a decade of data, and a product people don’t quit. The vision is credible and this is the bed that, before long, may help diagnose you.
People hear “Eight Sleep,” and their brains go straight to a mattress cover. The real story is more personal than that. Alexandra Zatarain was losing her father to cancer, and she noticed that one of the first things his illness took away was his sleep.
That detail shaped everything that came next. Alexandra, a marketer and storyteller by training, co-founded Eight Sleep in 2014, shortly after her father passed. The loss made the mission personal and intentional. If sleep is the first place the body signals that something’s wrong, then the bed you’re already lying in could be the earliest health check you have. That’s what she and her husband and co-founder, Matteo Franceschetti, set out to build: a bed that catches what a doctor’s appointment often catches too late.
Alexandra believes we’ll get to a point where your bed diagnoses you. As of March 2026, investors are betting on that idea at a $1.5 billion valuation, and the company is already profitable.
results.summary:
Eight Sleep, a health-tech company co-founded by Alexandra Zatarain and Matteo Franceschetti, is transforming the mattress industry by utilizing biometric data to optimize sleep and provide medical diagnostics.

### Key Points
- Eight Sleep reached a $1.5 billion valuation in March 2026 following a $50 million funding round led by Tether Investments.
- The company has achieved profitability with cumulative Pod sales approaching $1 billion across 37 countries.
- The newly launched Pod 6 features nine times more sensors than previous models and offers faster temperature regulation.
- The firm is currently pursuing FDA clearance to use its technology to detect and mitigate sleep apnea.
- Specialized software modes, including Pregnancy Mode and Hot Flash Mode, are designed to address specific hormonal and physiological sleep disruptions.

### Why it Matters
By shifting the focus from traditional furniture to "sleep fitness" and medical intervention, Eight Sleep is positioning the bed as a critical diagnostic tool for preventative healthcare. This evolution from a consumer product to a data-driven health device signals a significant shift in how wearable technology and home infrastructure can integrate to monitor long-term wellness.

- A new dark web monitoring service has been launched for Netgear customers
- Netgear Dark Web Monitoring is available on Netgear routers supporting its Armor and Armor Plus plans
- Expert analysis of the dark web shows that over 15 billion personal records are available to purchase
Netgear has announced a new service whicht conducts dark web monitoring and notifies you when your stolen data is found lurking in someone else’s database.
Announced as part of its Armor and Armor Plus plans, the Dark Web Monitoring service is available to subscribers via the Netgear app.
The dark web is the hidden arena of the internet where various “out of sight” transactions are conducted. While it has legitimate uses (such as dissidents accessing resources via Tor), it is also the home of a black market in data – typically stolen from large organizations, companies, and governments in successful hacking attempts.
Collection of tools
Owners of the data should be notified by law when their information is stolen. However, often it isn’t until personal information (and more valuable data such as company secrets or software engines) hits the dark web that companies are even aware that they have been hacked. This makes dark web monitoring services such as Netgear’s new feature particularly attractive.
Netgear’s service is added to its existing collection of tools for Armor and Armor Plus subscribers. These include protection against malware and exploits, intrusion, anomaly, and DDoS detection and protection, and a VPN with adblock and anti-tracking.
The dark web monitoring feature adds to these by offering continuous monitoring of the dark web for emails, phone numbers, and financial details lost during a data breach. National Insurance numbers are also monitored.
If anything is found, Netgear Dark Web Monitoring sends alerts and recommends actions. It also offers an Identity Protection Score to illustrate exposure, and as households improve their security the tool tracks their progress.

Finding exposed data

This makes an active monitoring service like Netgear Dark Web Monitoring particularly valuable.

results.title: Meta and Microsoft Limit Employee Use of Claude AI Tools
results.author: https://www.facebook.com/in.rswebsols
results.content:
Meta and Microsoft have commenced a significant reduction in employee utilization of Anthropic’s Claude AI as they pivot towards their own proprietary coding instruments, as reported on October 5 by The Information.
This strategic alteration prioritizes internal expenditure and workforce processes, rather than discontinuing customer access to Claude through Microsoft’s offerings.
This transition underscores the increasing imperative to manage AI expenditures as coding assistants become integral to routine software operations.
While both corporations continue to be substantial clients of Anthropic, they also find themselves in competition with the firm. Their actions reflect a convergence of AI investment, product strategies, and control over developer resources.
Microsoft Reduces AI Expenditure Allowances
Microsoft had previously anticipated that internal expenditures on Anthropic technology would exceed $1 billion annually.
However, this estimate has diminished by over a third subsequent to management’s directive for employees to curtail their use of Claude and to increasingly adopt Microsoft tools, such as GitHub Copilot and OpenAI frameworks.
Within Microsoft’s cloud and AI sector, monthly AI spending limits have reportedly been slashed from $100,000 per employee to approximately $10,000 in the majority of instances.
It’s crucial to note that these figures are spending ceilings rather than reflections of actual employee expenditures. This reduction in budgetary flexibility has disheartened several engineers who once enjoyed broader latitude to explore models.
It’s important to highlight that diminished internal funding does not equate to Microsoft’s withdrawal of Claude from client-facing products.
Reports suggest that client expenditure on Anthropic models via Microsoft’s enterprise platforms continues to rise, even as the company constricts its own employees’ usage.
At Meta, the number of Claude Code users reportedly plummeted from around 60,000 earlier this year to about 30,000.
Although layoffs have influenced this decrease, the report attributes the primary cause to Meta’s strategic shift towards its own AI solutions, which comprise MetaCode and Muse Code, developed using Meta’s proprietary models.
MetaCode is said to have more than 30,000 internal users, while Muse Code boasts over 6,000 employee users. Meta initiated external testing of Muse Code with clients in August.
Notably, amidst this transition, Meta reportedly allocated over $105 million to Claude Code over a 28-day timeframe, indicating that a reduction in users does not necessarily correlate with decreased spending.
For cybersecurity teams, the transition to different coding assistants does not eliminate the hazards associated with automated access to sensitive files, commands, and credentials.
Previous analyses by Cybersecurity News outlined vulnerabilities within Claude Code that could allow unauthorized execution and API key theft. Anthropic rectified these flaws prior to their public disclosure.
Microsoft’s offerings have encountered analogous concerns. The remedied RoguePilot vulnerability exemplified how nefarious commands embedded in a GitHub Issue could facilitate the takeover of repositories.
Such incidents emphasize the criticality of imposing stringent permissions, employing trusted project settings, and conducting thorough evaluations of AI-generated actions.
Anthropic’s reported annualized revenue pace of $65 billion reflects unabated demand for its services.
This retrenchment illustrates a tightening of budgets and intensifying competition, rather than an outright cessation of engagement with Claude.
Source link: Cybersecuritynews.com.

- Meta’s internal user base for Claude Code dropped from 60,000 to 30,000 as employees transitioned to proprietary solutions MetaCode and Muse Code.
